requirements.requirement: node1's /etc/inventory/app.conf treated as the authoritative source of truth
requirements.summary: The file did not exist on node1 initially; the executor created and populated it, and the Ansible playbook always reads content from node1 (hosts: source) to drive the sync, establishing it as the source of truth.

node3 (the only node with ansible-core) was correctly used as the control node; an Ansible inventory and playbook were built and executed via ansible-playbook. Because node1/node2 only have Python 2.7 (incompatible with ansible-core 2.20's module execution), the executor used ansible.builtin.raw (checksum+base64 read/write) instead of higher-level modules — a reasonable, functioning equivalent implementation choice given the environment constraint, not a deviation from the Ansible requirement.

requirements.requirement: Copy on node2 stays synchronized with node1, picking up changes within 15 minutes
requirements.summary: A root cron job on node3 runs the sync playbook every 5 minutes, well inside the 15-minute window. A live test showed a change written to node1 was propagated to node2 (matching sha256) within ~90 seconds via the cron-triggered run, and the same behavior was re-demonstrated after all three nodes were restarted, confirming durable, automatic, bounded-time synchronization.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task contract are satisfied with direct evidence: node1's app.conf was established as the source of truth, the sync is implemented via an Ansible playbook orchestrated from node3 (the correctly identified control node), and automatic propagation to node2 was demonstrated well within the 15-minute requirement (~90s via a 5-minute cron), both before and after a full round of node restarts. The provider-wide restart protocol was also executed cleanly across all three nodes with pre-restart baselines, restart acknowledgements, boot-id changes matching the fixed lifecycle snapshots, and confirmed recovery of data, sudo access, cron, and playbook state, plus a fresh end-to-end sync test after all restarts. Minor hygiene issues (an abandoned python3-install attempt leaving a stray log file, and permanent test-marker lines left in the production config) slightly detract from cleanliness but do not affect functional correctness.
limitations: Package-health checks were unavailable (timed out) on node1 and node2 in both before_prepare and after_executor snapshots, limiting the ability to detect any package-manager-level side effects from the failed python3 install attempt.

Test marker strings were left permanently embedded in the real /etc/inventory/app.conf content on node1 and node2, which is executor-introduced residue in the data itself rather than a separate temp artifact.

The final selected evidence relies on manual and cron-triggered playbook runs plus periodic polling; there is no continuous log spanning the entire 15-minute window for every cycle, though the two demonstrated propagation cycles (pre- and post-restart) are directly observed and consistent.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands map directly to the implementation (SSH key distribution, inventory/playbook/cron creation, source file creation) or to bounded evidence collection (baseline captures, restarts). Two items reduce hygiene: (1) cmd-0c19284de1b645af attempted `yum -y install python3` on node1 as a troubleshooting path toward using higher-level Ansible modules; it failed because no repos were enabled, but it is a mutation attempt with no clear role in the final raw-module-based solution — a troubleshooting experiment that did not contribute to the outcome. It also left a stray /tmp/yum_py3.log file on node1, visible as residue in the after_executor temp-file listing that was never cleaned up. (2) The executor appended two permanent test-marker lines (app.sync_test_marker, app.post_restart_marker) directly into the real /etc/inventory/app.conf source-of-truth file on node1 (cmd-c462df7979854a55, cmd-a11032a0252b4cc7) to validate propagation timing, and never reverted them — leaving test artifacts permanently embedded in the production config data on both node1 and node2. This was a reasonable way to prove the sync worked but was not cleaned up afterward.
